content: The administration of sodium picosulfate, magnesium oxide, and anhydrous citric acid can interfere with the absorption and metabolism of various drugs, leading to reduced efficacy or increased toxicity. Below are the detailed interactions: 1. Sodium picosulfate, magnesium oxide, and anhydrous citric acid reduce the absorption of omadacycline by inhibiting gastrointestinal (GI) absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is recommended. Multivalent cation-containing products can impair the absorption of tetracyclines, reducing their efficacy. Dosing of tetracyclines should be separated from these products. 2. Oxacillin decreases the effects of sodium picosulfate, magnesium oxide, and anhydrous citric acid by altering their metabolism. Caution should be exercised, and monitoring is advised. Co-administration with antibiotics reduces the efficacy of sodium picosulfate by altering colonic bacterial flora, which is necessary for its conversion to the active drug. 3. Oxaprozin and sodium picosulfate, magnesium oxide, and anhydrous citric acid may increase each other's toxicity. This interaction may be associated with fluid and electrolyte imbalances. Caution and monitoring are advised. 4. Sodium picosulfate, magnesium oxide, and anhydrous citric acid reduce the levels of penicillamine through cation binding in the GI tract. To avoid magnesium chelation, penicillamine should be taken at least 2 hours before and not less than 6 hours after the administration of sodium picosulfate, magnesium oxide, and anhydrous citric acid. 5. Penicillin G aqueous, penicillin G benzathine, penicillin G procaine, and penicillin VK reduce the effects of sodium picosulfate, magnesium oxide, and anhydrous citric acid by altering their metabolism. Caution and monitoring are recommended. Co-administration with antibiotics reduces the efficacy of sodium picosulfate by altering colonic bacterial flora needed for its activation. 6. Pentamidine, piperacillin, and polymyxin B reduce the effects of sodium picosulfate, magnesium oxide, and anhydrous citric acid by altering their metabolism. Caution and monitoring are advised. Antibiotics reduce the efficacy of sodium picosulfate by altering colonic bacterial flora required for its activation. 7. Sodium picosulfate, magnesium oxide, and anhydrous citric acid reduce the levels of polysaccharide iron through cation binding in the GI tract. To avoid magnesium chelation, polysaccharide iron should be taken at least 2 hours before and not less than 6 hours after the administration of sodium picosulfate, magnesium oxide, and anhydrous citric acid. 8. Prednisolone and prednisone may increase the toxicity of sodium picosulfate, magnesium oxide, and anhydrous citric acid. This interaction may be associated with fluid and electrolyte imbalances, such as hypokalemia. Caution and monitoring are recommended. 9. Quinupristin/dalfopristin, rifampin, rifapentine, streptomycin, sulfadiazine, sulfamethoxazole, and trimethoprim reduce the effects of sodium picosulfate, magnesium oxide, and anhydrous citric acid by altering their metabolism. Caution and monitoring are advised. Co-administration with antibiotics reduces the efficacy of sodium picosulfate by altering colonic bacterial flora required for its activation. 10. Sodium picosulfate, magnesium oxide, and anhydrous citric acid reduce the levels of tetracycline and tigecycline through cation binding in the GI tract. To avoid magnesium chelation, these drugs should be taken at least 2 hours before and not less than 6 hours after the administration of sodium picosulfate, magnesium oxide, and anhydrous citric acid. 11. Tobramycin, telavancin, and vancomycin reduce the effects of sodium picosulfate, magnesium oxide, and anhydrous citric acid by altering their metabolism. Caution and monitoring are recommended. Antibiotics reduce the efficacy of sodium picosulfate by altering colonic bacterial flora required for its activation. 12. Tolmetin, salsalate, sulfasalazine, and sulindac may increase the toxicity of sodium picosulfate, magnesium oxide, and anhydrous citric acid. This interaction may be associated with fluid and electrolyte imbalances. Caution and monitoring are advised. 13. Triamcinolone acetonide injectable suspension may increase the toxicity of sodium picosulfate, magnesium oxide, and anhydrous citric acid. This interaction may be associated with fluid and electrolyte imbalances, such as hypokalemia. Caution and monitoring are recommended. 14. Baloxavir marboxil levels are reduced by sodium picosulfate, magnesium oxide, and anhydrous citric acid due to cation binding in the GI tract. This interaction should be avoided, and alternative drugs should be considered. Baloxavir may bind to polyvalent cations, resulting in decreased absorption. Studies in monkeys have shown significantly decreased plasma levels with concurrent use of calcium, aluminum, or iron. Human studies have not been conducted. 15. Betamethasone may increase the toxicity of sodium picosulfate, magnesium oxide, and anhydrous citric acid. This interaction may be associated with fluid and electrolyte imbalances, such as hypokalemia. Caution and monitoring are recommended. 16. Capreomycin reduces the effects of sodium picosulfate, magnesium oxide, and anhydrous citric acid by altering their metabolism. Caution and monitoring are advised. Co-administration with antibiotics reduces the efficacy of sodium picosulfate by altering colonic bacterial flora required for its activation. 17. Sodium picosulfate, magnesium oxide, and anhydrous citric acid reduce the levels of carbonyl iron through cation binding in the GI tract. To avoid magnesium chelation, carbonyl iron should be taken at least 2 hours before and not less than 6 hours after the administration of sodium picosulfate, magnesium oxide, and anhydrous citric acid. 18. Cefaclor, cefadroxil, cefazolin, cefdinir, and cefditoren reduce the effects of sodium picosulfate, magnesium oxide, and anhydrous citric acid by altering their metabolism. Caution and monitoring are recommended. Co-administration with antibiotics reduces the efficacy of sodium picosulfate by altering colonic bacterial flora required for its activation. In all cases, close monitoring is essential to ensure therapeutic efficacy and minimize potential adverse effects.
